points.en: Gets the idea, studies the text, puts down everything, and starts collecting material, as steps one to four in that order.
Gathers other materials, arranges a tentative outline, broods over the message, writes it out in oral style, as steps five to eight.
Step nine is preparing to preach: prayer, restudy, and going over the sermon on one's feet.
Adds what each step accomplishes, such as writing the body first and the introduction last.
Names and describes all five methods: memorizing, reading, extemporaneous, limited notes, impromptu.
Gives a weakness for the methods, such as forgetting one word in memorizing, being tied to the page in reading, blunders in impromptu.
Gives a strength or fit for the methods, such as extemporaneous being liberating, and that no one method fits everyone.
Links preachers to methods, such as Edwards reading, Peale extemporaneous, Spurgeon sometimes impromptu.
Chooses two of the five half-truths and shows why each is incomplete when treated as the whole truth.
Gives balanced advice that corrects each, such as natural but with bad habits corrected, or filled with the subject while watching the audience.
Uses the lesson's reasons, such as some people being naturally dull, or God providing only after the preacher has made effort.
Optimum pitch is found about three to five notes above the lowest note one can hit.
Names the three inflections: downward for a completed thought, upward for question or excitement, circumflex for strong doubt or emphasis.
Reading fairy tales to children trains expressive inflection because we are naturally expressive with children but inhibited with adults.
Adds that pitch tends to rise with volume, so reach for a lower note when getting louder.
Faster talkers, around 180 words per minute, are more persuasive than slow or average ones at 120 to 150, so the greater danger is speaking too slowly.
A rate about twenty to twenty-five percent above average is ideal.
Pauses serve as punctuation, effect and emphasis, and a pause before beginning focuses attention.
Cites Jack Benny's long pause before a punch line, or nervousness making speech too fast.
Names at least four body topics from authority and confidence, appearance, movement, the face, eye contact, hands (and sincerity).
Explains what is at stake in each, such as nervous habits showing a lack of poise, or eye contact with individuals that audiences prefer.
Mentions Mehrabian's finding that communication is largely facial and vocal and that people believe actions over words.
Enthusiasm is the shared mark of great preachers (zeal, unction, fire), and it is not the same as volume or oratory.
Preaching from the soul and dominating the space describe enthusiasm as the preacher's presence occupying all the space he and the audience share.
Notes that students rate their energy too high, so videotape often shows far less than felt.
Prescribes at least five specific actions drawn from the unit, and ties each to a symptom of the nervous preacher.
Includes thorough preparation and rehearsing the sermon on his feet, plus prayer.
Includes delivery fixes from the unit, such as controlling nervous habits with deep breaths, speaking with Scripture's authority, composed pulpit presence, and letting hands rest at his sides.
Uses further unit advice, such as avoiding filler words like ah and you know, or practicing pitch and inflection.
Lists the nine steps in order: idea, study, put down everything, collect material, gather other materials, arrange, brood, write in oral style, prepare to preach.
For two chosen steps, explains why the order matters or what goes wrong if the step is skipped or reversed.
Uses lesson reasoning, such as the introduction last because the sermon develops in unexpected directions.
Prescribes varying pitch and inflection to avoid monotone, using the unit's teaching on optimum pitch and the three inflections.
Prescribes speaking faster than average, toward the ideal of twenty to twenty-five percent above average, with pauses.
Prescribes using the body, such as face, eye contact, gestures and movement, to add energy, and each change is something he can rehearse this week.
Gives practice like reading fairy tales aloud to a child.
